Where is the whale shark. When is the next feeding. Is this exhibit good for a four-year-old. Which way to the dolphins. The answers came from people standing on the floor, all day, repeating themselves. That is a reasonable way to run a visitor experience until you count the hours, and until you notice that the questions which genuinely need a person are waiting in the same queue as “where are the toilets”. Before Staff answered the same routine questions in person, all day. A visitor with an unusual question waited behind ten people asking for directions. After Routine questions are answered wherever the visitor is standing. Staff time goes to the questions and the moments that need a person. Georgia State University wanted to test whether an assistant could take that load, and asked us to build it. What we built A chatbot that knows the aquarium, rather than one that knows the internet. We collected the material visitors ask about and built a knowledge base from it. The chatbot uses retrieval-augmented generation: for every question it first finds the relevant pieces of the aquarium’s own content, then writes an answer from those pieces. This is the part that matters for a public-facing bot. Grounding every answer in retrieved source material is what stops it inventing a feeding time. A model answering from memory alone will confidently tell a visitor the wrong thing, and in a building full of families that is not an acceptable failure mode. The knowledge base is the part the aquarium controls: Content the staff own. Exhibits, animals, schedules, accessibility and wayfinding, in the aquarium’s own words. Updated without a developer. When a schedule changes or an exhibit opens, the content is updated and the chatbot answers from the new version. Answers that cite what they came from. Every response traces back to a piece of source material rather than to the model’s training data. Where it is now The chatbot is piloted inside the aquarium with real visitors. In pilot running with real visitors on the aquarium floor 5.0 Clutch rating for quality, schedule and cost On time delivered on the agreed schedule The routine questions get an immediate answer wherever the visitor is standing. A visitor who wants to know where the penguins are no longer has to find someone to ask, and the staff on the floor get their attention back for the conversations that are worth having in person. The project ran from March to May 2026. The client reviewed it on Clutch with five stars for quality, schedule, cost and willingness to refer. Recognize your own operation in this story?
